title: Cross and crucifix
hookLine: an empty cross, or Christ on it: churches choose differently

lines: ONE CHURCH: A FIGURE. ONE CHURCH: BARE WOOD.
cards: On a jeweler's tray, two silver necklaces, same chain, same shape. One is a plain cross: two bars, nothing else. The other carries a tiny figure, arms stretched wide, head bowed.
In one church, the big cross above the altar has that figure on it. Across the street, the cross on the wall is bare wood. Nobody in either building forgot anything.
Each one chose. And the two choices say the same sentence, with the stress on different words.

teach.h: AN INSTRUMENT OF DEATH, WORN ON A CHAIN.
teach.b: Day eighteen asked why an execution became the sign on the steeple. Today, two ways of showing it. First, the plain difference.
A crucifix is a cross with the figure of Christ on it; a cross on its own has nobody on it. Both point at the same death, an execution the letter to the Hebrews places outside the city gate.

That's the strange thing: an instrument of death ended up on necklaces and steeples. Paul wrote to the Galatians: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Next, the crucifix.
Catholic churches keep one on or near the altar, and Orthodox Christians often use crosses with Christ painted on them, like an icon.
Paul told the church in Corinth: "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified."
Some who pray before a crucifix say it keeps the cost in view: a real body, real nails, nothing tidied away. Then the empty cross.

teach.h: THE BARE CROSS: HE IS NOT HERE.
teach.b: In other churches, Protestant ones especially, the cross is bare. To those who choose it, the emptiness is the message.
In Matthew, the women come to the tomb at dawn, and the angel says: "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." The bare cross points to that morning. Last, side by side.
Churches with a crucifix still sing about the empty tomb; churches with a bare cross still read the story of the nails. One story: one holds the death in view, the other the morning after.
In both, the whole sentence gets said: he died, and he rose.

how: Catholic churches keep a crucifix on or near the altar, Orthodox churches often use crosses with Christ painted on them, and Protestant churches often display a plain cross; Christians of every kind may wear either on a chain.

games.q: you're Paul, arriving in Corinth, a city full of clever talkers. what do you decide to talk about?
o: the best arguments of the philosophers.
nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
only the miracles, since they impress people.
games.why: "I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." the crucifix keeps that same focus in view.

practice: Look at a cross, a necklace, a picture, a steeple out the window, or the one on the screen, and notice first whether it's empty or carries a figure.
Let your eyes move slowly along the upright beam, the crossbeam, the place where the two meet.
If you pray, you can pray in the words your own church uses before a cross; if you don't, simply look, and let it be a shape that carries a story.

wordCard.voice: Cross and crucifix. The bare shape, and the shape with Christ on it: two ways of showing one story.

orig.note: Greek: the New Testament's word for the cross Jesus died on.
